description: Taking on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator as a solo builder. The goal is simple: visualize Sun and Earth trajectories at potential Lunar South Pole landing sites to help assess power generation and communication links.
summary:
SELENE-X compares lunar landing sites and dates by showing when the Sun and Earth are above the horizon. The Sun gives power and Earth gives a direct radio link. Near the south pole both sit only 2° to 7° above the horizon, so a site can lose one or both for days. Using NASA NAIF SPICE data, it calculates Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation for any lunar site and date, finds every sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset to about one second, and combines them into power and communication windows. It offers a 3D Moon globe, elevation charts, an illustrated sky view with Earth’s phase, countdowns to sunset and Earthset, side-by-side site comparison, and an Artemis III requirements check.
My results match NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.007° in the tested south pole case. The Moon is modelled as a smooth sphere, so sunlight figures are upper limits. Slope and approach-lighting requirements are marked “not tested”, and NASA LOLA terrain data is planned. SELENE-X is open source (Apache 2.0), credits every NASA source, and uses no NASA logos or branding.
details:
SELENE-X compares lunar landing sites and dates by showing when the Sun and Earth are above the horizon. The Sun gives power and Earth gives a direct radio link. Near the south pole both sit only 2° to 7° above the horizon, so a site can lose one or both for days.

What it does: Using NASA NAIF SPICE data, it calculates Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation for any lunar site and date, finds every sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset to about one second, and combines them into power and communication windows. It offers a 3D Moon globe, elevation charts, an illustrated sky view with Earth’s phase, countdowns to sunset and Earthset, side-by-side site comparison, and an Artemis III requirements check.

Accuracy and limits: My results match NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.007° in the tested south pole case. The Moon is modelled as a smooth sphere, so sunlight figures are upper limits. Slope and approach-lighting requirements are marked “not tested”, and NASA LOLA terrain data is planned.

Equipment and tools:

  • Hardware: a personal Windows computer.
  • Data: NASA NAIF SPICE kernels (de440s.bsp, pck00011.tpc, naif0012.tls), checked against JPL Horizons. The Artemis III briefing (NTRS 20250009323) and a NASA Scientific Visualization Studio video (SVS 5228) are used as references and credited.
  • Software: Python, PyCharm, SpiceyPy, Streamlit, Plotly and NumPy.
  • Publishing: Git and GitHub for the code (Apache 2.0), and Streamlit Cloud for the live app.

Use of AI: I used Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant to help write and debug code, structure the app, and draft documentation. I ran and tested the code myself, compared the results with NASA JPL Horizons, and checked the sources and credits.

SELENE-X is open source, credits every NASA source, and uses no NASA logos or branding.
